speaker: Unknown
words: Interview is of Olive Randall, May, June 20th, 1975 at St. Maries, Idaho, by Irma Wood.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: What do you want to start with? Like. the things you enjoy about living in St. Maries or (unintelligible)?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, I think it's a small place. And where you know everyone.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: And I think that's an advantage, don't you? You know everybody in town and everybody a friend.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, that's, I think it's more enjoyable in a large place because, you know, you don't hardly know anyone. Your next door neighbor in these large cities.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Yes, but I think that's an advantage, definitely. How does your family life compare with the life when you was a child? Family life compare with the life when you was a child? Maybe, either financially or free time or.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, I was live, I was raised in a small place too, and everybody knew everyone those days, too. In the community where I grew up.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Did you, live on a farm or?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: On a homestead.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: On a homestead. You had a garden?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Had a garden and we lived, well, just out of Sandpoint a ways. I went to a rural school until I went to high school in Sandpoint.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Let's see. How long did you know the man you married?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Three years. I knew him three years before we were married.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Was there any unusual circumstances about meeting him, or? Like, where did you meet him?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Oh, he came to a dance and, and he, of all the girls, he chose me to dance with first. So, I don't know. I guess he just loved me.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Yeah, well. Let's see. What did you expect? What was your expectations of marriage? I don't know, just be married and.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, the main thing was to love each other and get along, and, I always figured it was a 50-50.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: (Unintelligible) 50-50. Yeah. A 50-50 arrangement. Yeah. And it says what medical services were available to you when you were having your children?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, we had the, there was the doctors, you know.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Did the doctor come to your house or did you go to the hospital?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: We went to the hospital.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: The hospital. In Sandpoint.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Yes. And in St. Maries, too, when my children were born.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: What factors most affected the number of children you had? Just don't know about that. Where did you get your knowledge about childbirth? I didn't see these questions. About, and child rearing.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, I don't know. I just, I suppose from older women.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Probably, maybe your mother, or?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Oh, yes. I suppose my mother, and neighbor ladies.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: How has the role of your children changed since you had children? Okay, did the older children change since you had the children?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, they've grown up and, and, are on their own, have families of their own. I guess that's.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Now you have grand.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: And grandchildren.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Great grandchildren.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: And great grandchildren, which I enjoy.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: And it says, what do you personally do for recreation?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, I belong to so many lodges and 2 or 3 clubs. And the senior citizens, we dance every Saturday, you know.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Oh, you do. That's a nice thing to do. Do you go to the Elks to dance?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, I haven't in quite a few years because my sons aren't here, you know. I used to when they were here, but. Occasionally we'd go over here to the Eagles and dance, but mostly down to center.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Oh, that's great.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: New.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Relaxation. And, thinking back, what are some of the things you have done to help support your family? And I suppose that would be raise the garden and keep the house.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: You know, just made a home for them and raised a nice garden and.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Did you have cows, or?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, oh, yes, we had cows and chickens.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Took care of them.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: And horses.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Let's see, how do you. Has there been, ever been a time when you have had the major responsibility of your family?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, yes. Part of the time when the children were growing up and going to school here in town, my husband worked out in the timber and.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Was he gone a week at a time?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: He was gone a week at a time. So.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Yeah, then you had to have the full responsibility of.
Of the children.
But you haven't ever had to help support them.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Oh no, I never did have to, no.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: And, what community activities are you, have you been involved in and why?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Oh, I.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Through all those clubs in the.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: In the clubs, that home demonstration club that I belonged to. I almost try to remember the home demonstration club. I didn't put that down. I belonged to that too.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: And. I heard you mention senior citizens and that (unintelligible).

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, I've always taken an active part in my senior citizens' club and helped to get it going, you know.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: And the grandmothers' club? Could you tell us a little bit about that?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, I have gone quite a number of years to that. I have never been the, yes, I've been the grandmother of the year, too.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Oh, that's great. What do you do with the grandmothers' club?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, we have a business meeting once a month, and then the second meeting of the month, we play cards. And so. We've always had quite an active club.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: And, would you tell something about the senior citizens' club?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well. We have, a potluck dinner once a month, and, every Saturday afternoon we dance.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Oh, you do?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: And, let's see. We have, two meetings a month, business meetings, and, once a month, why, we gather and all take part in printing out a little paper. We print out a little paper called The Sparkler.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Oh, the senior citizens (unintelligible). Oh, well, that's great.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: And, of course, there's, two of the ladies that kind of go ahead and, and, plan the articles to be put in the paper, and then we all gather there on a certain date and address those and send them out in the mail.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Oh. And who did they go to?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: To all our members. And we have about 300 members.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Oh, well, that's quite a bit of doing.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: And then we, kind of take turn about and two of us will, take care of, the club for a week at a time and do the janitor work, sell the rummage and, answer the telephone and.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: And, somebody told me that the club wasn't funded by any money you earned.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: No, we had government help to start with, and, we gave food sales and rummage sales and all different things to bring in money. And we finally. Well, then we, the businessmen of the town donated money to help us get started. And, we soon was able to, get away from the government help, and, so we paid for our building, which was $16,000. We paid for that in just a little over a year.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: And you earned all your own money.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: And now we're independent and, and, and, rummage that we sell helps pay the, expenses. And also we have, every Tuesday night, Bingo, which brings in money. And for a long time, we, saved the aluminum beer cans and sold those and got quite a bit of money. We, sell, we go through our rummage and, pick up the, things that don't sell well and, make good rags and sell them to the (unintelligible).

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: And that brings in quite a little bit for us.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: (Unintelligible).

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Came to St. Maries and went to work for the Milwaukie Lumber Company. And, as scaling. And, he worked up by Fernwood. And then they changed and decided to go up Alder Creek to log. So my husband found a homestead cabin for us to live in, and. So we moved up there, just took a, some bedding and dishes and clothing. And sort of camped out all winter. And we didn't have, only one near neighbor. And I thought I'd just moved to the end of the world when I got there, six miles from the railroad. Well, but anyway, we spent a good winter, and, yeah, there was a post office about a mile and a half from us and a little grocery store called Sylvester's Post Office.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Oh, was that there in Fernwood?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: No, up Alder Creek.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Up Alder Creek.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: What they call the Benewah, out in the Benewah Country. And, we used to buy fresh meat and eggs from this little store.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Talk to me, tell about the, the shuttling?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Oh. Well, (unintelligible), the part that my neighbor wanted me to tell was, how I came from Spokane on the train, and change trains here in St. Maries and went up the branch line and got off at the mouth of Alder Creek. And rode a long train about four miles up the canyon and ate lunch at our logging camp then rode the log train up another 2 or 3 miles. And then, that's where we went to find this cabin and moved into it.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: Well, but you shut it off, I'll tell you. I'm. So when I start. When you said you were lonesome in Spokane.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, I lived alone in Spokane a month, and. And was real lonesome. And I told my husband that I would gladly live in any kind of a little cabin if I could be close to where he could be home. And so he found a cabin for us to live in. It was a homestead cabin. And. So I came to St. Maries on the train, and then I came on up to the branch line on the train, and a log train met me at the mouth of Alder Creek. And I rode the log train for about four miles and got off and ate lunch at a logging camp, and then got back on the log train and rode, oh, about three miles farther, and then finally got off and walked in about an inch of snow in high-heeled shoes. And finally came to the cabin. But the funny part of it was the way I was dressed. I had on a real nice dress, black satin skirt, (unintelligible) waist, and a black plush coat with a big fur collar. And there I was, riding on the greasy engine and, I don't know why I didn't have presence of mind to have rubbers on. I'm leaving Spokane, and knowing I was gone to the woods.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: But you said the hobble skirt was kind of hard to.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Well, now I had to climb up in the engine, which was a, a real tall step and I had on a hobble skirt, had to pull myself up to sit on that greasy engine. But we finally came to the log cabin and and lived there all winter, and I thought I had just come to the end of civilization. I was six miles from a railroad. Never had been that far away, out in the woods. And had one neighbor, an elderly lady that hadn't been to St. Maries only once in eight years, so she couldn't tell me very many interesting things. But we were about a mile and a half from a little grocery store and post office. And we used to buy fresh meat and eggs there. So we managed to live all winter, and I did lots of fancy work and read lots of stories and. And I thought if I ever live through this winter, I'll be glad to go back to town. But I lived there nine years.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: I suppose, did you have a wood stove?

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Oh, yes, we had a wood stove.

speaker: Irma Wood
words: It was probably Jerry Brunner.

speaker: Olive Randall
words: Had a nice spring close to the. Well, we finally brought land out there and lived for nine years out there. And then the youngsters who, were old enough to go to school and so I moved into town. And I've lived in St. Maries ever since.
